sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The 5-30 December 1456 earthquake is the largest destructive event occurred in the Italian peninsula and one of the strongest of the entire seismic history of Italy. Its very large damage area, its magnitude and to the fact that the cumulative intensity field contains effects from multiple shocks, in the past prevented the constraining of discrete events and, therefore, the identification of plausible causative fault(s). The area affected by the 1456 sequence extends from Central Abruzzo (to the north) to Apulia (in southeastern Italy) and from the Adriatic to the Tyrrhenian coasts.
Although no specific source could be recognized in the past, in the literature it was assumed that the 1456 earthquake had ruptured across several ca. NW-SE trending normal fault segments, by proximity and apparent similarity to those responsible for the better known Southern Apennines-top earthquakes (Magri and Molin, 1983; Meletti et al., 1988; Cecic et al., 1996; Troise et al., 1998; Teramo et al., 1999). On the grounds of (a) the time-and-space analysis of the earthquake sub-events, (b) the damage scenario unfit for NW-SE trending dip-slip causative sources, (c) instrumental evidence from adjoining strong earthquakes and (d) the presence of deep-seated regional ca. E-W structures, we suggest that these multiple pene-contemporaneous sub-events were generated and/or controlled by oblique right-lateral reactivation of segments of deep E-W seismogenic sources.
The complexity of the damage pattern resulting from the 1456 sequence can therefore be the result of (1) source multiplicity (i.e. combination of the shaking effects of faulting on three or more parallel E-W strands), (2) depth of the sources (below 15 km, calling for a strong regional propagation that emphasizes the role of local anomalies) and (3) dynamic relation with large tectonic units of the Southern Apennines. While main destructive (M > 6.5) activity in the core of the thrustbelt occurs within the first 10/12 km, the proposed sources activated by the 1456 sub-events ruptured in the lower portion of the seismogenic layer.
We believe that a seismogenic macroregion, characterized by oblique dextral slip occurring along E-W preferential planes, dominates the structural domain bounded by the NW-SE trending system of main extensional faults (to the west) and the buried external Apennine front (to the east). Such sources, capable of generating destructive earthquakes (as demonstrated by the Irpinia 1930, M 6.7 event), would thus be the western expression of the seismicity alignments, roughly E-W oriented, marked by the intermediate earthquakes occurred in the Apulian foreland.
Our hypothesis invokes stress interaction between multiple sources falling within neighboring domains. Such interaction is more commonly observed at the very short or very long scale (like the Irpinia 1980 sequence or the relationship between this earthquake and the Potenza 1990/1991 sequence; Troise et al., 1998). However, we believe that the seismic crisis of 1456, made of multiple destructive shocks across a uniquely wide area within a 30-45 days timespan, may represent a similar example of complex relation among large events occurring in the deeper Adriatic crust.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) How many are the primary shocks that made up the moment release of the 1456 sequence?
2) Is the inferred right-lateral, oblique kinematics the only plausible one for the mainshocks?
3) How did the mainshocks interact at such distances? And how did these events interact (if so) with adjoining, major seismogenic normal faults in the core of the Southern Apennines?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Magri and Molin (1983)
These authors are the first ones to collect the contemporary sources and historiographic chronicles of the 5 Dec 1456 earthquake. They state that this was one of the most important natural events of the Italian seismic history. They also underline that this major earthquake is of key relevance to the seismotectonic interpretation of the Apennines.
Meletti et al. (1988)
These authors made a thorough revision of all the available historiography and some new sources, to desume the sequence and the damage pattern. They desumed that the very broad intensity distribution is due to the quasi-contemporaneous activation of multiple earthquake sources.
Guidoboni and Comastri (2005)
These authors advanced the Historiographic research on the 1456 earthquake sequence, re-evaluating virtually all information for all localities listed in the available macroseismic dataset. This led them to change several intensity values and to propose that the overall damage results from the quasi-contemporaneous occurrence of four separate events, recognized on the basis of historiographic information.
Fracassi and Valensise (2007)
These authors performed a critical re-appraisal of the newly available intensity data from Guidoboni and Comastri (2005) and previous studies. They propose that the 1456 sequence is composed of various sub-events but that only three main events are responsible for the major damage, between 5 and 30 Dec. 1456. On the ground of the known historical seismicity in the southern Apennines and the information from available subsurface geology, they propose three seismogenic sources for the three main events. They believe that the 1456 sequence hints at a seismogenic style that falls between the mainly extensional Apennines axis and the mainly right-lateral strike-slip kinematics occurring in the Apulian foreland.
